chapter_theme: Songs at Vellikaram (வெள்ளிகரம்), the 'silver town' (வெள்ளிநகர்) among paddy fields near Valli's hill: the poet confesses his infatuation with women and his body ruled by the five senses, and asks for the silence beyond words, for the instruction that melts the heart, and for words to proclaim Murugan; the praise turns again and again on Valli and on Murugan himself made a lover.
structure_note: 656 and 657 share a closing line on the blooming lotus of Vellikaram; 658 to 663 are a run of short songs tightly built on doubled ல்ல and ள்ள, with shared refrains (658, 659: அடையலர் செல்வம் அளறிடை செல்ல; 660, 661: வெய்ய சைய வில்லி சொல்லை வெல்ல வல்ல; 662, 663: வெள்ளிமணி மாட மல்குதிரு வீதி). Women (658 to 661, 663), the senses and silence (656), proclaiming the god (657, 659, 662), and 664, a praise song of Murugan the madal-riding lover, Kannappa and Krishna.

656.reading: The poet tells how, in this body swarmed by the five that follow Brahma's ordaining, in the wave-girt world, battered by the five quarrelsome ones and stumbling, a servant in distress, he asks that heart, word and body reach their end, the world's infatuation leave him, and, with himself gone, to gain Murugan's feet, Murugan tell him the one thing that marks the bound of silence. The praise pictures Valli's breasts, face and ears like vallai leaves, names Murugan who wrote his emerald form on the madal and stood in Valli's field, the guru of self-born Siva of the silver mountain, at Vellikaram of the blooming lotus.
656.nuance: எனது அற நினது கழல் பெற: the feet are gained when 'mine' ends. மவுன எல்லை குறிப்பது ஒன்று புகல்வாயே asks to be told the one word that points to silence, a paradox the book returns to. The ஐவர் are the five senses, pictured as quarrelsome masters. The opening (அடல் அரி மகவு விதி) is hard to divide.

657.reading: The poet asks whether the golden feet can be gained except by words that make all the world know Murugan's emblems: the dancing peacock that broke the peaks, the fresh kadamba, the small sword-like vel, the lotus faces, the fighting cock in his hand, and his name as Valli's husband of the Aivana hill. The praise names him the incomparable son of Siva, the guru of the discourse beyond words, the beautiful one under the old nelli tree where the cowherds pass with their herds, the great life of Siva who wears Ganga, the moon, konrai and vilvam, at Vellikaram.
657.nuance: The plea makes proclaiming the god the only road to his feet (மொழியின் அல்லது ... பெறலாமோ), while the praise calls him the teacher of a discourse beyond words (நிர்வசன ப்ரசங்க குருநாதா): speech is the poet's way, wordlessness the god's teaching.

658.reading: The poet tells of desiring women whose jasmine-white teeth and sweet speech, ear-rings, slender waists and breasts draw him into a union that brings worry, and asks Murugan instead to give gently his red feet, adorned with a garland of clear verse and fragrant flowers. The praise names Valli, born of the lone spotted doe with which the ascetic sage played, whose millet Murugan slowly ate in the field on Valli's hill, and Murugan of the beautiful silver town who destroys the assemblies of those who preach false paths and makes enemies' wealth sink in the mire.
658.nuance: The plea offers a garland of verse (கவிமாலை) for the feet, the poet's song set against the union. அவநெறி சொல்லும் அவரவை கொல்லும் may again point to the defeat of the Jains, though no sect is named. The doubled ல்ல and ள்ள rhythm makes several words hard to divide.

659.reading: The poet asks whether his heart, cunning and melting at women's eyes that push at their ear-rings and their jasmine smiles, will not learn, while life remains in the world, to say with learning and understanding that Murugan is the treasure Uma gave. The praise names Valli's bridegroom, the hero of the old emerald peacock that measured the world's bounds, the warrior who threw the vel to split the hill, the life of the silver town amid fields.
659.nuance: உலகு உயிர் உள்ள பொழுதே: the time to learn to praise is now, while life lasts. The heart that melts (உருகிட) for women is the same heart the poet would have melt in praise.

660.reading: The poet tells how, giving his wealth into the hands of a deceitful, clever woman, his gems, grain, silver, learning and wealthy kin all vanished, and of the indescribable misery of the mire to which the five senses lead, and asks the true Lord to give his red feet. The praise names Murugan infatuated by the parrot speech of Valli, daughter of the generous spotted doe, the life of the silver town where white conches climb in the dark fields as the farmers slowly reap the paddy, and the Lord able to overcome the word of the fierce bowman of the mountain.
660.nuance: கையில் அள்ளி பொருள் ஈய: the wealth goes by the handful into the woman's hand, so the courtesan's trade is named, and with it go not only goods but learning and kin. The refrain வெய்ய சைய வில்லி சொல்லை வெல்ல வல்ல probably names Siva, whose bow was the mountain, and may refer to Murugan's teaching of Siva; the allusion is not certain.

661.reading: The poet asks whether he will take delight in the words of a creeper-like woman who mocks him while making him infatuated with her painted breasts, slender waist, deceitful eyes that push at her ear-rings, and dark hair full of jasmine. The praise names Murugan the beloved son infatuated with divine Valli, daughter of the spotted doe on the stony hill of millet, true to the true and false to the false, the life of the white silver town.
661.nuance: மெய்யர் மெய்ய பொய்யர் பொய்ய: Murugan is real to those who are real and unreal to the false, an epithet that answers the woman's deceit (கள்ள விழி) in the plea. எள்ளல் செய்யும்: the woman mocks the man she infatuates.

662.reading: The poet calls himself one without a way to salvation, who in his need went to people who will not share even a sesame seed's worth, unlike those ashamed to say 'there is none' and who never refuse from what they have; who cannot put Murugan's names into verse, does not understand the boundless first cause, and is a liar who tends a sagging body; and asks by what power the pure feet will rule him without letting him go. The praise names the vel that struck the dark mountain so the demons died and the gods lived, the lord of the creeper of Valli's hill, the Kumaresa on the peacock wearing vellil and kadamba, at the silver town of jewelled mansions.
662.nuance: இல்லையென நாணி உள்ளதின் மறாமல் describes the true giver, ashamed to say 'none', who does not refuse from what he has, the Kural's ideal (223). Whether the poet confesses begging from misers (பகிராரை ... நாடி) or his own failure to share depends on how the line is divided.

663.reading: The poet, a lone dog who ran like a boy after the slow beauty of thin-waisted women and fell into the sea of infatuation, asks that, to be saved, Murugan once speak to him the instruction that makes the heart melt and seek, and give him the joyous play that is neither being nor non-being, beyond delusion. The praise names the lord who rules the whole earth, Valli's bridegroom on Valli's hill, whose vel set the seven seas aflame and felled the demon lords with their mountain, at the silver town.
663.nuance: உள்ளதும் இலாது அல்லது: the bliss asked for is beyond both 'is' and 'is not', the language of the Siddhanta and Vedanta for the Lord. உபதேசம் is the guru's instruction, asked for directly. The division of மல்லதவிரோத is uncertain.

664.reading: A song of praise in long, intricate lines: it pictures Murugan in Valli's millet field, her lotus face and arrow eyes, the god who lost his strength and, infatuated, mounted the palmyra horse, the lustful one who is our Lord; names him son of the pure Siva who ate the meat the hunter tasted first and offered with 'see, these are sweet'; and tells of his uncle as Krishna, delighting Yashoda, rolling the mortar he was tied to, growing until he pierced the sky as Mahabali feared, at the silver town where conches play in the fields.
664.nuance: மாலாய் மடலேறும் காமுக எம்பிரானே: Murugan himself takes the lover's last resort, riding the madal, and is called 'the lustful one' and 'our Lord' in one breath, as in 641 and 656. The hunter whose spittle-tasted meat Siva ate is Kannappar, the type of love that ignores rule. Several phrases (வாராய்பதி காதங் காதரை ஒன்முரும், நூறாயிர பேதஞ் சாதமொழிந்த) are obscure.

links.note: Both define the giver by his shame at the word 'none': the Kural's man of good family does not utter the misery of 'I have nothing' and gives without refusing, and 662 names those ashamed to say 'there is none', who do not refuse from what they have, using the same word for misery (எவ்வம்).
The Kural calls the palmyra horse the only defence of those who suffer in love; 664 has Murugan himself, infatuated in Valli's field, mount it, the god taking the lover's last resort.

656 asks that, with 'mine' gone (எனது அற), he gain the feet and be told the word that marks the bound of silence. The Kural says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods'. Both make the end of 'mine' the condition of the highest gain, the Kural as renunciation, the song as reaching the feet.

657 asks whether the golden feet can be gained other than by words that make all the world know Murugan's emblems (அகிலமும் உணர மொழிதரு மொழியின் அல்லது). The Kural says the two dark deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise (பொருள்சேர் புகழ் புரிந்தார்). Both make proclaiming the Lord the working means, not ornament; the song adds that his own teaching is beyond words (நிர்வசன ப்ரசங்க).

658 asks Murugan to accept, adorning his red feet, a garland of clear verse with fragrant flowers (தெள்ளு கவிமாலை கடிமலர்). Tirumular, having nothing to show the Lord morning and evening, offers the song that cools the heart as the oblation (உள்ளம் குளிர்விக்கும் பாட்டவி). Both make the song itself the offering.

659 asks whether his heart will not learn, while life remains in the world (உலகுயிர் உள்ள பொழுதே), to say that Murugan is Uma's son. The Kural says good deeds must be hurried to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள் மேல் வாராமுன்). Both set the deadline at the end of life; for the song the deed to be done before it is speech itself, praise.

660 tells how, putting wealth by the handful into a deceitful woman's hand (கள்ள முள்ள ... கையில் அள்ளி பொருள் ஈய), his gems, grain, silver, learning and wealthy kin all vanished. The Kural says double-minded women, liquor and dice are the company of those whom Fortune has left (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு). The song is a narrative of the Kural's verdict, with learning and kin lost alongside wealth.

661 calls Murugan true to the true and false to the false (மெய்யர் மெய்ய பொய்யர் பொய்ய). Tirumular's horse of salvation, traditionally the breath, gives a hold to the true and leaps and throws the false (மெய்யர்க்குப் பற்றுக்கொடுக்கும் ... பொய்யரைத் துள்ளி விழுத்திடும்). The same pairing of மெய்யர் and பொய்யர் describes a means of release that answers each person according to his truth; in the song that answers the woman's deceit.

663 asks for a joyous play that is neither being nor non-being (உள்ளதும் இலாது அல்லது) and for the teaching that melts the heart. Tirumular says the Lord becomes what is and what is not yet is neither (இல்லதும் உள்ளதுமாய் அன்றாம்), far beyond whatever is said, but becomes life of life when understood. The song asks for the state the Tirumanthiram describes, in the same terms.

source_issues: Song 664: two corrupt characters, in உலு஡கல (line 533, probably உலூகல, 'mortar') and வயலு஡டிடை (line 537, probably வயலூடிடை).
The heading is வெள்ளிகரம், while the songs name the town வெள்ளிநகர் (658 to 664) and வெள்ளிகரம் (656, 657).
